extracted.intended_audience: scholars, students, and readers interested in digital culture and internet memes
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for studying, categorizing, and assessing internet memes and scholarship about them, with emphasis on what makes memes significant, successful, and research-worthy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Memes are research-worthy because they embody Web 2.0 participatory culture
rubrics_metrics.description: Internet memes are worthy of research because they embody the many embedded aspects of Web 2.0 participatory culture and make elements of digital culture explicit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Studying memes can reveal communicative roles, social and political beliefs, and features of participatory culture; use this as justification for academic attention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear definitions and distinctions (memes vs. virals)
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide comprehensive and specific definitions; distinguish memes from 'virals' — virals become memes when ordinary Internet users alter the original content for their own communicative purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be explicit about definitional boundaries. The crucial difference is personalization/derivation: when users alter popular content it shifts from viral to memetic, which is central to claims about memetic power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operationalize 'memetic success' as high volume of derivatives
rubrics_metrics.description: Define success for memetic content as content that 'generates a high volume of derivatives' (Shifman 73).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use publicly accessible popularity measures and platform data (e.g., YouTube playlist info, Know Your Meme database) to identify highly replicated memetic videos and photos.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mixed-methods empirical approach (qualitative + quantitative)
rubrics_metrics.description: Combine qualitative and quantitative research methods to study memes: identify successful memes quantitatively, then perform qualitative analyses of their features and functions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: select a corpus of memetic videos/photos using popularity measures, then categorize common features and analyze meanings and discourse in depth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feature analysis: incongruity predicts replication and alteration
rubrics_metrics.description: Memes that are more incongruous with expectations are more likely to be spread and altered by ordinary people, producing personalized meanings and sparking discourse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Categorize memes by features (e.g., incongruity) and test association with derivative volume; use this as a theorized mechanism for memetic uptake.

rubrics_metrics.name: Categorize meme genres and map digital literacy requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify distinct meme genres (Shifman identifies nine) and recognize that each genre requires different levels and types of digital literacy to participate in.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing participation, assess the genre-specific skills and competencies required (see examples like LOLcats needing specific language conventions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Define and value pillars of digital literacy for memetic participation
rubrics_metrics.description: Sharing, imitating, remixing, and using popularity measures have become highly valued pillars of participatory culture and are expected from a 'digitally literate' netizen (23).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure or account for these behaviors when evaluating participation or the spread of memes; they signal competence and inclusion in memetic discourse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical skill requirements for participation
rubrics_metrics.description: Participation in certain meme genres requires technical skills: Photoshop for memetic photos, video production/editing for memetic videos, and platform literacy for posting/sharing/replying.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess accessibility and participation barriers by documenting required tools/skills for producing and modifying memes in each genre.

rubrics_metrics.name: Memes as polyvocal discourse and personalization
rubrics_metrics.description: Iterations of memes represent a variety of views and opinions shared through polyvocal memetic discourse; ordinary people interject their perspectives into memes, enabling social discourse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze derivative variations to map different voices, perspectives, and meanings produced by participatory remixing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political memes function by participating in normative debate
rubrics_metrics.description: Political memes are about making a point—participating in a normative debate about how the world should look and the best way to get there (120).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate political memes by the clarity and persuasiveness of the point they make, their circulation, and how they mobilize or construct normative claims; compare democratic and non-democratic contexts (e.g., 'We are the 99 Percent' vs. Chinese River Crab/Mud Horse).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider historical/offline antecedents to strengthen arguments
rubrics_metrics.description: Including offline historical memes (e.g., 'Kilroy Was Here') demonstrates that the meme concept is not new and can validate contemporary arguments about meme significance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To bolster claims about memes' social role and historical depth, include multiple historical/offline examples and trace continuities with online memetic behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Global and translation functions of memes
rubrics_metrics.description: Memes have global functions and can be translated across cultures; analysis should account for cross-cultural transmission and transformation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study how memes travel, are adapted, and gain new meanings in different cultural contexts; include comparative or translational analysis in global meme studies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency and referral to primary sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Be transparent about data sources and encourage readers to consult original sites and materials; the author suggests readers visit cited sites and sources themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document data collection methods, provide links to exemplar memes, and include notes/references by chapter and page numbers to enhance reproducibility and further research.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of illustrative examples (images, links) to support claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Including photos of memes and references to websites to view examples is useful for illustrating analytical points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide visual examples and direct links when making claims about genres, formats, or specific memes; this aids reader comprehension and supports analytic claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide organized reference aids (glossary, hubs, lists of genres/features)
rubrics_metrics.description: A glossary summarizing terms and a short list of meme hubs are valuable; expanding these to include organized lists of meme genres and attributes contributing to memetic success would help readers recall and differentiate findings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include summative appendices or tables listing genres, features linked to success, and methodological notes to make research more usable for readers and future projects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scholarly rigor: comprehensive literature review and proper citations
rubrics_metrics.description: Ground arguments in a comprehensive literature review, referencing well-recognized authors and providing detailed notes and citations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the book or study situates itself within existing scholarship, cites relevant works, and offers end-of-chapter notes with page references for further consultation.
